source.title: Sample, Mix, or Verify? Allocating Test-Time Compute under Imperfect Verifiers

record.tranche_reason: The study uses an adapted compute-optimal rule from Singhi et al. as an allocation baseline and compares power-law forecasts for inference-time success. It does not test the claim’s pretraining cross-entropy laws or parameter/token/compute allocation laws.
record.gate_note: The study measures and forecasts test-time verified success and coverage, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss. Its own power-law forecast comparisons are recorded as findings about a related construct under fits_no_version. The Singhi-rule allocation comparisons are adapted to this study’s settings; the paper explicitly says they do not test Singhi et al.’s original claim. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study's outcomes are inference-time coverage and verified success as a function of the number of samples, rollouts or agent systems. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or training compute. Its power-law comparisons concern the repeated-sampling coverage law of Brown et al., a related but different construct. The Singhi et al. rule is a test-time solve/verify allocation rule, not a pretraining parameter/token allocation. The paper says conclusions about that baseline concern transfer to its settings, not Singhi's original claim. No version V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that a pilot-calibrated planner (SPLIT) allocates test-time compute within 0.02–0.8 points of the hindsight optimum, while fixed rules lose 2.5–20 points. They find SPLIT beats power-law forecasting when verifiers cap success, but not for pure coverage or argmax selection. They stress that their claims rest on decisions and mechanisms, not forecasting accuracy. They draw no conclusions about pretraining scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study forecasts inference-time coverage and verified success over sample or rollout counts, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss across parameter, token or training-compute scales. It also compares a test-time allocation heuristic adapted from Singhi et al.; the paper says this does not test their original claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Forecast performance changes with the target and selection setting: the power law is worse for several verified-selection settings but better for pure coverage and SWE-bench argmax selection. Verifier type and modelling task-varying verifier accuracy also affect forecasts.

fits_no_version.finding: A power law fitted to pilot selection curves over-predicts verified success, because an imperfect verifier caps success. MAE is 7.6 vs 1.9 under a simulated verifier, with smaller gaps for real tests and SWE-bench thresholds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Power-law forecasts of test-time verified success fail when an imperfect verifier caps success.

fits_no_version.finding: For pure coverage, the power law is as good as or better than the mechanistic forecast: 2.6 vs 3.3, and tied on the agent pool (p=0.57). This is consistent with heavy-tailed difficulty.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time coverage follows a power law in the number of samples that extrapolates well.

fits_no_version.finding: For SWE-bench argmax selection, the power law has lower mean error than SPLIT (1.58 vs 3.28).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Power-law extrapolation can outperform mechanistic forecasts for some test-time selection rules.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says the code will be released publicly)
record.problems: The measured outcomes are inference-time success or coverage rather than pretraining loss. For the agent-pool horizon, systems are treated as exchangeable attempts, which the authors distinguish from repeated sampling by one agent. The authors also note that their same-agent rollout horizon is limited and that capability drift makes small, unrepresentative pilots fail.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for allocation-regret comparisons against the adapted Singhi et al. rule: the paper says these comparisons concern transfer to its test-time settings, not the original compute-optimal claim. Other tables and figures report inference-time allocation or mechanism results, not the pretraining-loss versions.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolating pretraining loss from small runs to large ones.
Power-law loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining scale or loss.
Fit-dependence of pretraining-loss exponents and of the compute-optimal split.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T4 / uses_without_test classification is reasonable; it could arguably be T6, since the study cites test-time power laws rather than the pretraining laws in V1–V7. The rows are correctly unlinked. Omitting the Singhi-rule allocation rows is justified: that rule concerns test-time solve/verify allocation, not pretraining N/D allocation.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy versus parameter count, training tokens or training compute.
Prediction of larger-run held-out pretraining loss from smaller pretraining runs.
Compute-optimal pretraining parameter and token counts as functions of training compute.
Effects of depth, width and other architecture details on pretraining loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance as a function of pretraining scale or loss.
Whether pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal parameter/token splits depend on fitting choices and setup.

rows.subject: MATH + CodeContests, sim. verifier (pilot 32)
rows.operation_detail: Forecast selection success beyond pilot sample counts and compare forecast MAE with a power law fitted to the pilot selection curve.
rows.measure: Extrapolation MAE over N beyond the pilot (percentage points)
rows.note: Aggregate result for MATH and CodeContests with a simulated verifier; this measures verified inference success, not pretraining loss.
rows.check: Measures forecast error for test-time verified success against sample count N, not pretraining loss. Linking to none is correct.

rows.subject: MATH + CodeContests
rows.operation_detail: Forecast coverage beyond pilot sample counts and compare forecast MAE with a power law fitted to coverage.
rows.measure: Extrapolation MAE over N beyond the pilot (percentage points)

rows.check: Coverage against sample count, not pretraining loss. Correctly unlinked.
